issues.legal_issue: Election under a will arises only when the legatee receives a benefit under the will that the legatee would not otherwise be entitled to receive.
material_facts: The properties covered by the will were joint family properties of the testator and his son.
The son had an interest in the properties and would have received the residue by survivorship even without the will.
The son obtained probate and carried out the will’s provisions, and it was argued that this conduct amounted to an election.
issues.conclusion: The son’s conduct did not amount to an election because he received no benefit under the will to which he was not already entitled.
issues.legal_principle: Indian Succession Act, 1925, section 180, requires a person whose property is disposed of by a will to choose between confirming the disposition and dissenting from it; on dissent, the person must give up benefits provided by the will. Applying the principle described in Halsbury’s Laws of England, Third Edition, volume 14, paragraph 1091, election arises when a legatee must choose between retaining the legatee’s own property and taking a benefit conferred by the will. It does not arise where the legatee would receive the same property independently of the will.

predicates.purported_election_under_will: A person who received property under a will was said to have elected to accept the will’s disposition.
predicates.legatee_already_entitled_to_property: The legatee would have received the property through an existing interest in it even without the will.
predicates.no_additional_will_benefit: The will gave the legatee no benefit that the legatee would not otherwise have received.

issues.definition: When a purported election under a will concerns property the legatee was already entitled to receive, and the will adds no benefit, the legatee’s acceptance of the will does not amount to an election.

issues.legal_issue: A will cannot change joint family property into the absolute property of the son when the testator lacked the right to dispose of the whole property.
material_facts: The properties were found to be joint family properties of the testator and his son.
The testator’s will gave the residue to his son, but the testator was not entitled to dispose of the entire joint family property.
The son obtained probate and carried out the will’s provisions.
issues.conclusion: The property retained its character as joint family property in the son’s hands insofar as his male issue was concerned.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, a father’s share in ancestral property remains ancestral property as regards his male issue, who take an interest by birth. The Court relied on Mulla’s Hindu Law, Thirteenth Edition, paragraphs 223(2), 223(4), and 224, and held that a father’s will could not change the character of joint family property which he lacked the right to dispose of as a whole.

predicates.property_was_joint_family_property: The property belonged to a joint family of the testator and his son.
predicates.testator_lacked_right_to_dispose_of_enti: The testator did not have the right to dispose of the entire property by will.
predicates.will_purported_to_give_property_to_son: The testator’s will purported to give the property or its residue to his son.

issues.definition: When joint family property is purportedly given to a son by a will that the testator had no right to make as to the whole property, the property retains its joint family character.

issues.legal_issue: An adopted son’s independent interest in joint family property is not defeated by an election made by his adoptive father under a will.
material_facts: The property retained its character as joint family property in the adoptive father’s hands insofar as his male issue was concerned.
The son was adopted by the holder of the property and thereby acquired an interest in the joint family property.
The defendants argued that the adoptive father’s acceptance of the will bound the adopted son as well.
issues.conclusion: The adopted son’s interest was independent of his adoptive father, so he was not bound by any election the father might have made under the will.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, a son takes an interest in ancestral property by birth, and that interest is independent of his father; he does not claim that interest through his father. The Court relied on Mulla’s Hindu Law, Thirteenth Edition, paragraph 224, and applied that principle to the adopted son’s interest upon adoption.

predicates.property_was_joint_family_property: The property was held as joint family property in the adoptive father’s hands.
predicates.adopted_son_joined_family: A son was adopted into the family holding the property and acquired an interest in that property.
predicates.father_was_treated_as_having_elected_und: The father was alleged or assumed to have elected to accept the will’s disposition.

issues.definition: When an adopted son acquires an interest in joint family property and his father is treated as having elected under a will, the son’s independent interest is not bound by that election.
